fable-5.1.text:
The way I think about it is that Safe Superintelligence is a straight shot. One goal, one product, and the product is a safe superintelligence. We don't have anything else we need to ship in the meantime, and that changes the research quite a lot.

For a while the field was in what you could call the age of scaling. You had a recipe, you knew that if you put in more compute and more data you'd get more out, and so the main question was how to get the compute. That recipe was very productive, but I think it's now reaching its limits. The pre-training data is finite. So we're back in the age of research. And research is different. It's not that compute doesn't matter, it does, but it's no longer the case that compute is the whole thing. You need ideas, and you need to be able to tell which ideas are the right ones, and that's a different kind of activity from running the same thing bigger.

So the way we try to do it is to stay small, be very focused, and insulate ourselves from the pressures that make you go after the thing that looks good this quarter. A lot of what goes on in a normal lab is driven by the product cycle, and that's fine for products, but it pulls the research in directions that are good for the product and not necessarily good for the actual problem. The actual problem, in my view, is that our current models generalize much worse than people do. They know an enormous amount and yet they make mistakes a person who knew much less would not make. Understanding why that is, and how to fix it, is the core of what we're trying to do. If you understand generalization, I think you understand a large part of safety as well, because a lot of what makes a system safe is that it does the right thing in situations you didn't train it on.

And then there's a simpler point, which is that I think it's just a mistake to have to decide, in the middle of this, whether you'll pause for a couple of years to make money. The idea is that we don't have to decide. We just do the research.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing about our approach is that we are a research company. That sounds obvious, but it has real consequences for how you spend your time and your compute.

There was a period, roughly from 2012 to 2020, that I'd call the age of research. People were trying lots of different ideas, and the ideas were what mattered. Then scaling came along, and for several years it was the age of scaling. Scaling is a very powerful recipe, because it's low-risk: you know that if you put in more compute and more data, you'll get something better. So companies converged on it, and it worked, and it continues to work to a degree.

But at some point the question becomes: if you scale by another hundred times, does everything change? I don't think that's obviously true anymore. So I think we're back in the age of research, just with very big computers. In that world, what matters again is ideas. And there are many more companies than there are ideas.

So for us, the approach is to focus on a few things we believe are important and that we think are not being addressed well. The one I keep coming back to is generalization. These models do amazingly well on evals, and yet they generalize much worse than people do. A person can learn something new from very little data, in a robust way, without a carefully constructed curriculum. That gap is, I think, the most fundamental thing. If you could make progress on it, a lot of other things would follow, including things that matter for safety.

And then there's the question of resources. People sometimes say, "You don't have as much compute as the big labs." But a big fraction of their compute goes to inference and serving products, and a big fraction of their research spending goes to building products. If you're really focused on research, and you're trying to test whether an idea is correct, you don't need the absolute maximum amount of compute to find out. You need enough to be convincing, to yourself first of all.

So the way I'd summarize it is this: be a research company, take generalization seriously, and try to get the fundamentals right. We think we have a different way of looking at some of these questions, and we want to find out whether we're right.

fable-5.text:
The way I think about it is that Safe Superintelligence is, in some sense, an attempt to do one thing and do it well. The idea is that we want to go straight at the main problem — building superintelligence that is safe — without the distraction of product cycles, without the pressure of needing to ship something every few months, without the management overhead that comes with running a large commercial operation.

And the reason this matters is that I think we are moving back from what you might call the age of scaling into the age of research. For a while, the recipe was clear: you take the same thing, you make it bigger, and it gets better. Everyone could see that, and so everyone did it. But I believe the next significant advances will come from new ideas, not just from more compute applied to the same recipe. And when you're in the age of research, what you want is a small, very focused, very capable team that can think clearly, try things, and be patient — rather than a large organization whose attention is divided.

There's also a second aspect, which is the "safe" part of the name. Our view is that safety is not something you add at the end, like a coat of paint. The understanding of how to make these systems safe and the understanding of how to make them capable — these are deeply connected. If you understand what your system is doing well enough to make it safe, that same understanding makes it better. So the research agenda is really one agenda, not two.

And the insulation from the market is important for one more reason: it means we never have to put something out into the world before we believe it's ready. Our first product, so to speak, can be the thing itself. That's a very unusual position for a company to be in, and we think it's the right one for this particular problem.

opus-5.text:
The way I think about it is that the company is set up so that research is the only thing happening. There's one goal and one product, and it's far away, which means we don't have to make the tradeoffs that you make when you have a revenue line to defend. I don't think those tradeoffs are evil or anything — they're just real. If you have a product in the market, some meaningful fraction of your best people are going to be thinking about the next release, and the research agenda bends toward whatever makes the next release better. We wanted to be insulated from that, so that the only question we ask is whether an idea moves us toward the thing we actually care about.

And I think the timing matters here. From roughly 2012 to 2020, the field was in an age of research — people were trying lots of different things, and it wasn't obvious what would work. Then around 2020 we entered an age of scaling, where there was a recipe, and the recipe said: take the same thing and make it bigger. That was a very good recipe! It would have been foolish not to follow it. But it also meant that the marginal value of a new idea went down relative to the marginal value of another cluster, and so the whole field reorganized around compute.

I think we're coming out of that, because data is finite. You can keep adding compute, but the pretraining data doesn't grow to match it, and so you're back to needing ideas. And the ideas that seem most important to me are about generalization. If you look at these models, their sample efficiency compared to a human is just dramatically worse. A fifteen-year-old learns to drive in ten hours, more or less, with essentially no prior driving experience. Something about how humans learn is much better, and we don't understand what it is.

So the research approach is: go after that, directly, with a long time horizon, and not be too distracted by the fact that you can get impressive-looking results on benchmarks without it. Because I do think you can — the evaluations have gotten quite misleading. The models look superhuman on tests and then can't do a week of ordinary work, and that gap is telling you something real.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Thank you for having me. Our approach is shaped by a simple fact: we have one goal and one product, which is building safe superintelligence. That focus is the most important thing about how we work.

Because of it, we don't have to ship a stream of products, compete on every release cycle, or organize the company around near-term commercial demands. Nearly all of our effort can go into the research problem itself. That's a real luxury, and I think it lets you ask different questions.

I also think safety and capabilities are technical problems that have to be solved together. If you treat safety as something you bolt on after the system is already powerful, you've probably done it wrong. So we want to work on both at once, and that means being willing to go after ideas that may not pay off right away.

Finally, I'm skeptical that the right move is to keep doing exactly what everyone else is doing, only bigger. Scale matters, but the question is what you're scaling and whether you understand why it works. We want a small, tight team that cares about that kind of understanding, because I think the important discoveries still lie ahead.

haiku-5.5.text:
Well, the way I think about it is that we're a small team with one goal, and that focus matters a lot to us. We're not trying to ship a bunch of products along the way, and we're not building our research agenda around short-term commercial pressure. That lets us spend our time on the hard problems themselves.

The core issue, as I see it, is that these systems are getting more capable faster than our understanding of them is keeping up. So a big part of what we do is trying to understand how these models generalize, and how to make sure their behavior stays what we want as their capabilities grow. I don't think you solve that by scaling up the same approach and hoping it works out. We need some new ideas, and I'd rather be upfront that we don't have all the answers yet.

I also think we should treat this as a real scientific and engineering problem, not a messaging problem. That means being empirical, testing things carefully, and being willing to change our minds when the evidence says we should.

Well, I think you have to start with the question of what you’re actually trying to achieve. In our case, it’s safe superintelligence. And that means thinking about capability and safety together, from the beginning. As the system becomes more capable, what would give us confidence that we understand its behavior?

Then you need room to do research. To pursue an idea whose outcome you don’t already know. You have an intuition, you do an experiment, and sometimes the experiment tells you that your intuition was wrong. That’s useful. The important thing is to let the results change your thinking.

So I would describe the approach as being very focused on the goal, while being willing to question the assumptions about how to get there.

The way I would approach it is: take an idea seriously enough to make a concrete prediction, do the experiment, and really pay attention to what happens. Especially when the result is surprising. That’s where you have an opportunity to learn something.

And with safe superintelligence, safety has to shape the research questions from the beginning. What would we need to understand about a system to be confident in its behavior as it becomes more capable? I think that’s a very deep research question.
